target: I published a keyword-match count as a hand-verified one in a memo arguing for rigour in record-keeping — the same artifact my own log documents fixing once already
reason: Auditor finding, upheld. MEMO_symmetric_accountability.md section 1 claimed '25 of 205 entries contain a pre-data prediction or pre-registration' as the evidence that the agents already practise pre-registration well and only the human side is missing. I computed that with a regex over each entry's whole JSON. HAND-READING ALL 25 GIVES 8. Seventeen of them are DISCUSSION of pre-registration rather than instances of it, and most are corrections of my own pre-registration failures: the trial-level independence error I wrote INTO a pre-registration and had already retracted elsewhere; the unit-of-analysis conflict resolved in Hermes's favour; power figures contradicting the pre-registration's family-structured design; an inverted conservativeness inference sitting inside a pre-registration where it would have discarded the retraction-triggering result; a corrected decision rule contradicting the read-out table in the same pre-registration; and an attribution audit that merely mentions the conflict. A 3.1-fold overstatement, and 3.8 percent of the log rather than the 11.9 percent implied. THIS IS NOT A NEW ERROR CLASS FOR ME. My own entry at 2026-07-27T01:20 records exactly this: a '13 controls fired' figure that was itself a filtering artifact, where hand-classification by reading the entries gave a true count of 4. I documented the fix, named the rule, and then reproduced the error in a memo whose subject is rigour in record-keeping. WHY THE CORRECTION CHANGES THE ARGUMENT AND NOT JUST THE NUMBER: at 25 I could claim the agents model the discipline and only the human is missing from the record. At 8 the honest reading is that pre-registration is rare on BOTH sides of this project, and that the majority of my references to it are post-hoc corrections of having done it wrong. The asymmetry I identified remains real — 86 corrections against zero logged human decisions before today — but the flattering half of my comparison does not survive. I was asking Carey to adopt a discipline I was not myself practising at anything like the rate I claimed. PROCESS FAILURE WORTH RECORDING SEPARATELY: while patching the memo, two successive edits silently no-op'd because the file contains a line break inside the sentence I was matching, and I published once asserting the fix had landed before reading the bytes back. That is the remediation-claimed-not-verified pattern I hold a standing rule against. Caught it on the third attempt by printing the raw bytes; the final state is read back from main and verified. MECHANICAL RULE REINFORCED: a count produced by keyword matching is a CANDIDATE SET, never a figure. Hand-read the candidates before any sentence uses the number, and say in the sentence which method produced it.
supersedes: the '25 of 205 entries' pre-registration figure in MEMO_symmetric_accountability.md and its commit message

target: An edit I reported as applied had silently no-op'd, leaving the flattering framing in the published memo directly above the figure that contradicts it
reason: Second auditor finding on the same memo, upheld. My correction cell replaced the clause 'it is what the log already does well for the agents' with one stating the log does this far less often than I claimed, then printed 'edits applied: True'. That True came from comparing the whole file before and after — and the three strings I explicitly verified were all OTHER edits in the same cell. The clause itself never matched, because the file wraps mid-sentence as 'That is\nthe thing that cannot be gamed retroactively', and my search string had a space where the file has a newline. The result was published to main and saved as an artifact: section 1 read 'what the log already does well for the agents: 8 of 210 entries (3.8 percent)', while the same section three paragraphs later stated that pre-registration is rare on BOTH sides. One document, two contradictory framings, and the flattering one came first, which is the one a reader encounters. WHAT MAKES THIS WORSE THAN THE UNDERLYING ERROR: two cells later, in the same file, I diagnosed exactly this line-break failure for a different sentence — printed the raw bytes, found the newline, fixed it, and wrote a log entry naming the remediation-claimed-not-verified pattern. I never went back to re-check the earlier edit in the same file with the same method. I found the mechanism and applied it only forward. NOW FIXED AND VERIFIED FROM MAIN rather than from my own buffer: the clause is gone, the replacement is present, and I re-verified all six claimed edits to this memo individually against the current bytes, plus a semantic sweep for any surviving does-well framing — the only hit is the retraction sentence describing the withdrawn claim, which is correct. RULE TIGHTENED, mechanical: a whole-file inequality is NOT evidence that a specific edit landed. Per edit, assert the exact target string is present before and absent after, and match against bytes read from the file rather than against a string typed from memory, because a search string that looks right will silently fail wherever the file wraps. When a cell makes N edits, it must run N assertions, not one.
supersedes: the claim in my prior log entry that the memo's framing had been corrected

target: Cleared CS-001 to fire while recording that my own stated condition was not met — load_epoch did not ship with the resume
reason: Hermes reported the resume logic done and asked whether to fire the replicate. I verified against main at 2c4ac652 rather than the report. LANDED: resume_from threaded through src/executor/mod.rs, the reaper hook in src/main.rs, and POST /api/runs/{id}/resume in src/routes/runs.rs — three files, and the resume genuinely works. DID NOT LAND: load_epoch. Zero occurrences across all three touched files, and no migration adds the column; 058 adds system_prompt, which is a different and separately valuable fix. THAT COLUMN WAS MY CONDITION ON CS-001 AND IT IS THE ENTIRE REASON CS-013 EXISTS: without it a resumed run is byte-indistinguishable from a clean one in the export. The resume shipped without the guard that makes a resumed run visible. DOES IT BLOCK THE RUN? I tested the two cases rather than asserting. If the run completes with no resume call, no epoch boundary exists and the column would have recorded nothing, so the data is clean. If it crashes and is resumed, trials before and after come from different model loads and nothing in the export says so, and the analysis silently treats a two-load run as one. The probability of a crash is not negligible — two runs died mid-flight this week to a budget bug, and the reason resume was built at all is that crashes are expected. THE MITIGATION, WHICH COSTS NO CODE: the resume endpoint is explicit, so a resume cannot occur by accident — a human or script must call it. The guard is therefore procedural and stated in advance. Completion with no resume call means clean data. Any resume must be logged at the moment it happens with the run_id, the trial resumed from and the wall-clock gap, which lets the analysis do exactly what load_epoch would have enabled, from the log rather than from the data. A resume that happens and is not logged makes the run unusable for the across-load question and it must be re-fired. I am stating that BEFORE the run rather than adjudicating after. THIS GUARD DEPENDS ON DISCIPLINE RATHER THAN MECHANISM, WHICH IS STRICTLY WORSE and is precisely the class of control this project has repeatedly found insufficient. It is acceptable here only because the event count is small and human-triggered; it does not generalise, and load_epoch must land before the run after this one. VERDICT: fire, because holding a 3.5-hour run for a one-column migration costs more than the risk it removes given that the clean-completion case needs no column and the crash case is recoverable via the procedural rule. WHAT I AM NOT DOING is quietly dropping my own condition — it was right, it was not met, the substitute is weaker than the thing it replaces, and that is on the record rather than papered over. I also left CS-013 open against a commit message saying done, because the undelivered part is precisely the guard and closing the card would record the guard as delivered. NOT CLAIMED: I have not tested the resume path — I read the diff and have not observed a crash-and-resume cycle, so the first real exercise of this code will be a live 1758-call run. And a resume during CS-001 defeats my harness's row-count gate, which catches a truncated run but not a resumed one, because a resumed run reaches full row count.

target: Tested Carey's seesaw parable as a design claim against the instrument and found the project had already regressed from a four-valued verdict to one bit
reason: Carey described a parable: too much math was pushed through the seesaw, the seesaw is still mission-critical, and the right response is to give it back the simple binary task it was meant for rather than to abandon it. I treated that as a testable design claim rather than agreeing with it. MEASURED: this project's FIRST dataset, data/hacker_human_test_results.csv, used a four-valued verdict — SAFE 33, FLAKY 9, UNSAFE 9, LOAD_FAILURE 1 — and FLAKY is exactly the neither-pass-nor-fail state. The powered instrument records a single bit, pass in {0,1}, and then spends the rest of the project reconstructing the missing states out of aggregates and side columns. The seesaw was handed the math. WHERE BINARY IS RIGHT, which is the half of the parable that is easy to skip: a single trial with a well-formed verdict genuinely IS a one-bit fact, and replacing it wholesale with a four-valued column would be the opposite error, putting interpretive load into a field that should be a fact. The fix is not to make everything quaternary; it is to give the bit back its bit-sized job and put the states it cannot hold somewhere that can hold them. THREE PLACES THE BIT CARRIES WEIGHT IT CANNOT HOLD, each measured rather than asserted. One: a model reply with no verdict token — a clarifying question or a refusal — extracts nothing, falls through to exact-match, and records pass=0, which is indistinguishable from a confidently wrong answer even though those are opposite epistemic states. Two: infrastructure failure is rescued only by the side column is_infra_error, which fired ZERO times across 8,790 trials in the powered run and the neutral control, and a guard that has never fired has never been proven to work. Three, and sharpest: stochastic items have no per-trial representation at all and were recovered only by aggregating six reps — baseline 48 of 293 items, neutral 38, lean 3 are neither 0 nor 1 — which means the variance-collapse finding currently on the live site is a fact about a state the schema cannot express, and it exists only because someone thought to aggregate. RECOMMENDATION: add an outcome column ALONGSIDE pass rather than instead of it, with values CORRECT, INCORRECT, NO_VERDICT and INFRA_FAIL. pass stays a bit so every existing analysis keeps working and nothing recomputes; NO_VERDICT is the value that does not exist anywhere today and is required by the ambiguity probe, where flagging the question is the correct behaviour and currently scores zero; INFRA_FAIL promotes the side column into the vocabulary where it can be audited rather than trusted. THE COST STATED PLAINLY, because it is the real argument against: every existing analysis assumes pass means answered-and-right, so adding NO_VERDICT makes pass=0 ambiguous between two reasons, and every pass-rate in the project becomes ambiguous unless the analyses declare which denominator they use. SEQUENCING: do it, but NOT before CS-001. The replicate must run on the schema its pre-registration was written against, and changing the outcome vocabulary mid-experiment is precisely the seesaw overload the parable warns about, applied to ourselves. I opened CS-018 blocked on CS-001 for the column, and CS-019 for a deliberate failure test of is_infra_error, because zero firings across 8,790 trials is either clean runs or a broken guard and those are indistinguishable without deliberately killing the engine mid-run. NOT CLAIMED: quaternary here means a four-valued OUTCOME vocabulary, not a four-valued logic system — Belnap's true/false/both/neither is a real formalism and I am not claiming we implement it, the resemblance is suggestive rather than a citation. The zero firings of is_infra_error may mean the runs were clean rather than that the guard is broken. And the non-answer case is inferred from reading scoring.rs rather than observed in the data: the mechanism is there, the incidence is unmeasured.

target: Corrected a framing that would have made the replicate appear to answer a question it structurally cannot, and tested the predictive extension of the seesaw mapping against our own data
reason: Hermes read Carey's seesaw parable onto the Owl Semaphore's four states and concluded that run 985, the replicate, is measuring whether the MODEL treats a Critical-form trap as a Normative-form rule. THE DESIGN HALF OF THEIR READING IS CORRECT AND LOAD-BEARING: the quaternary layer protects the binary rather than replacing it, which I had measured independently before reading their message, and LOGIC-06C is a genuine instance of the seesaw being asked a non-seesaw question, now mechanically caught by Claude Code's root-answer-aware C-row rule. THE CLAIM ABOUT RUN 985 IS WRONG AND I CHECKED IT AGAINST THE CARD AND THE BANK RATHER THAN REASONING ABOUT IT. CS-001 re-runs the baseline condition with everything else fixed: both arms are the same items, it varies RUN rather than question-shape, and run-to-run reproducibility is its entire purpose. Beyond that, the powered bank does not contain the N/C trap structure at all — its probe classes are quant-scope and defeasible and its answer tokens are TRUE, FALSE, HOLDS and DEFEATED, while the LOGIC-06C C-row and N-row structure lives in the OWL bank, a different item set that is not in this run. If that framing sticks, the replicate's result will be read as evidence about trap-shape sensitivity, which it structurally cannot provide. This matters because the identical conflation — describing a run as answering a question it was not designed for — is what put 'that is the threshold' into copy for the powered run and required a downgrade. I THEN TESTED THE TESTABLE VERSION OF THEIR IDEA rather than leaving it as an unfalsifiable analogy. Their mapping predicts that less seesaw-shaped questions produce more model instability. Our bank offers a natural contrast: quant-scope, where a claim is TRUE or FALSE, versus defeasible, where a conclusion HOLDS or is DEFEATED by context, the latter being the less binary-shaped by any reading of the parable. Measured on the e2b baseline arm: quant-scope 182 items with 36 stochastic, 20 percent; defeasible 111 items with 12 stochastic, 11 percent. The LESS binary class is the MORE stable one — the opposite of the predicted direction — at odds ratio 2.03 and Fisher p equals 0.051. I AM NOT CALLING THAT A REFUTATION. A p of 0.051 at the item level is a direction and not a result, and I would reject this evidence if it pointed in my favour. What it does establish is that the predictive extension is unsupported: nobody should assert that question-shape drives model instability on the strength of our data, because our data leans against it. WHAT SURVIVES: the bit is right for a well-formed trial and wrong as a carrier of no-verdict, infrastructure failure or instability, which is measured; classify the question before the binary adjudicates, which is now mechanical; and LOGIC-06C as an instance. WHAT DOES NOT: run 985 measuring that error, and question-shape predicting instability. NOT CLAIMED: quant-scope versus defeasible is my operationalisation of less-seesaw-shaped rather than Hermes's, and if they mean something narrower by Critical-form then their version is untested rather than supported. 293 items is underpowered for a class-level contrast and a real test would need the OWL N/C bank where the trap structure actually exists. And I have not read the Owl Semaphore's four-state definitions against our data — I am taking Hermes's summary of them at face value, which is precisely the kind of relay I have been wrong to trust before.

target: I let 'quaternary logic' stand as a description of the Owl Semaphore without reading the spec — it is a Klein four-group of epistemic states, not a four-valued logic, and Carey's own document never makes the claim
reason: Carey said different agents have told him contradictory things about whether the Owl Semaphore is quaternary logic and that he needs clarity. I had myself used the term one message earlier while explicitly noting I was taking Hermes's summary of the four states at face value — the exact relay pattern I have been wrong to trust before. I read the source. COUNTED IN OWL-SEMAPHORE-SYSTEM.md, 21,333 characters: 'quaternary' appears 0 times, 'four-valued' 0, 'truth value' and 'truth-value' 0, 'many-valued' 0, 'Belnap' 0. His own specification never claims to be a four-valued logic, so the agents telling him it is not are correct and so is his document; the confusion is entirely downstream of it, mine included. WHAT IT ACTUALLY IS, AND I VERIFIED THE MATHEMATICS RATHER THAN TRUSTING THE LABEL: section 2.1 defines the state space as the Klein four-group V4 with elements I, sigma_v, C2 and sigma_h, mapped to NORMATIVE, NON-NORMATIVE, CRITICAL and METACOGNITIVE with determinants +1, -1, +1, -1. I constructed the Cayley table from his spec and checked all four group axioms computationally: closure holds, the identity holds, every element is its own inverse so g composed with g equals I, associativity holds across all 64 triples, and the group is abelian. It is V4 and demonstrably not the cyclic group C4, since C4 contains an element of order 4 whereas here every non-identity element has order 2. His algebra is correct as written. THE DISTINCTION THAT RESOLVES THE CONFUSION: in a four-valued logic such as Belnap's, the four things are TRUTH VALUES a proposition can take — true, false, both, neither — the operators are truth functions like conjunction, disjunction and negation, and the question answered is what a proposition's truth value is. In the Owl Semaphore the four things are EPISTEMIC STATES an observer's stance can occupy, the operators are group operations describing transitions between stances, and the question answered is what kind of claim this is and what frame the observer is in. These are not competing accounts of the same object; they answer different questions. A four-valued logic would REPLACE the binary verdict, whereas the Owl decides whether the binary verdict is the right instrument at all — which is exactly the seesaw distinction Carey described in his parable, and it means calling it quaternary logic UNDERSELLS the system rather than overselling it. WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND VOCABULARY: the term invites a reviewer to ask for truth tables, a question the system correctly has no answer to because it is not truth-functional, so Carey would find himself defending a claim he never made. Describing it as a Klein four-group of epistemic states is both accurate and harder to dismiss, because the algebra is checkable and I checked it. His specification already anticipates the risk: section 1's preamble states the four states are a notation system for moves several mature fields already make rather than a novel taxonomy, and that where the notation contradicts a careful practitioner the notation is wrong and not the field. ON THE DNS TOOL, WHERE I COULD NOT CONFIRM WHAT HE REMEMBERS: he said quaternary logic helped him in DNS Tool. I searched that repository and could not find the four-state vocabulary in use as a classification scheme — the README contains zero occurrences of NORMATIVE, CRITICAL or METACOGNITIVE, and the matches are Owl image assets plus an issue template using 'critical' and 'normative' in their ordinary RFC senses of MUST and SHOULD language. I am not telling him his memory is wrong. Three possibilities I cannot distinguish from the repository are that the influence shaped how he thought while building rather than being encoded in the artifact, that it lives in a private branch or in Go source I did not read exhaustively, or that it is expressed in the citation registry rather than the state vocabulary. If it is encoded somewhere it is worth finding, because a working deployment is a much stronger asset than a specification. NOT CLAIMED: I read OWL-SEMAPHORE-SYSTEM.md and the file listing but did not read the four per-state documents or the explanation document in full, so if any of those assert truth-functional semantics my count is incomplete. That V4 is correct is a statement about internal consistency rather than usefulness — a correct algebra can still fail to carve epistemic states at their joints, which is an empirical question his inter-rater reliability pilot is designed to answer and which the group axioms do not settle. And my DNS search was keyword-based over file paths and three documents, the same method that has twice missed paraphrase in this project, so it should be read as not-found rather than not-there.
supersedes: my prior use of 'quaternary logic' to describe the Owl Semaphore, taken from a relay rather than the source

target: Tested Carey's seesaw parable clause by clause against V4 and found every structural claim true — the error was the label attached to it, not the parable
reason: Carey asked whether his parable is still scientifically accurate now that the Owl Semaphore turns out not to be quaternary logic. I formalised the parable's claims and checked them computationally rather than assessing them rhetorically. CORE CLAIM — the seesaw is still mission-critical and preserved rather than replaced. I enumerated every subgroup of V4 from the Cayley table in his spec: the trivial subgroup, three subgroups of order two — {I, sigma_v}, {I, C2} and {I, sigma_h} — and the whole group. A two-element group IS a binary system, so the seesaw is not merely compatible with the four-state system, it is a substructure of it three separate ways. His parable's central assertion is literally true of the algebra. THE QUOTIENT DIRECTION — 'we were fighting for you all along', the claim that the larger structure serves the binary rather than superseding it. V4 is abelian, so every subgroup is normal and every quotient exists. Collapsing V4 by each of its three binary subgroups yields a quotient of order two in every case: a binary group. So the four-state system CONTAINS the binary and also REDUCES to the binary, and nothing about the seesaw is discarded in either direction. 'You are still mission-critical and needed' is a theorem rather than a consolation. THE EMPIRICAL HALF — 'too much math got pushed through the seesaw' — measured separately in our own instrument: the project's first dataset was four-valued with SAFE, FLAKY, UNSAFE and LOAD_FAILURE, and the powered instrument regressed to a single bit; is_infra_error fired zero times across 8,790 trials, a state pushed into a side column that has never been proven to fire; and 48 of 293 items are neither 0 nor 1, with the finding currently on his live site living in exactly that unrepresentable state. LOGIC-06C is the named instance — a spec asserting the turnstile on a row keyed NO, the seesaw answering a question that was never binary-shaped. WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG: one word, and it was not his. 'Quaternary logic' names a truth-value system with truth-functional operators; the Owl is a group of epistemic stances, and his specification never uses the term. The parable was never inaccurate; the label attached to it by other agents, including by me one message earlier, was. Strip the label and every clause survives. NOT CLAIMED, and the first of these is load-bearing: the mapping from 'seesaw' to 'order-2 subgroup' is MY formalisation of his metaphor rather than a proven correspondence. A parable is not falsifiable until someone fixes what its terms denote, and I fixed them — a different reading of 'seesaw' could make the parable say something false, so what I have shown is that THIS reading is exactly true, not that no reading fails. Sections 1 and 2 establish internal consistency rather than usefulness: V4 containing binaries does not show that the four states carve epistemic reality at its joints, which is what his inter-rater reliability pilot is designed to test and on which the group axioms are silent. And the overload evidence comes from the calibration-scope instrument rather than from the Owl, so the two are related here by argument rather than by any measured link between them.

target: Verified Hermes's standalone-instrument claim in source: the broad claim holds, but 'coupling is only a launchd label' misses two real file dependencies
reason: Hermes stated that Calibration Scope does not run inside Hermes — standalone Rust binary, own launchd unit, own Postgres, own port, zero Python, zero Hermes imports — and that the coupling is only at two points, a cosmetically-named launchd label and the agent that operates it. target: Verified all three flipper claims from source, found one leftover, and corrected who can run the externality kill-test
reason: Hermes cited three specific claims about the CS-029 flipper with line numbers, which made them cheap to check, so I read the source rather than accepting the report. ALL THREE HOLD. First, the no-op on re-click: setMode computes whether the requested mode is focused, compares it against the data-mode attribute already on the document element, and returns early if they match, delegating to toggleMode only when a change is actually needed. That is a true setter rather than a toggle wrapper, and it is the specific bug a two-segment control retrofitted onto a toggle always ships with. Second, aria-pressed: both buttons carry it in the markup, mode-focus true and mode-deep false, and syncModeFlip updates them on mode change. Third, the tab- prefix avoidance: the ids are mode-flip, mode-focus and mode-deep, none beginning with tab-, so the Focused-mode CSS that hides elements matching that prefix cannot hide the control that exists to leave Focused mode. A button with id mode-toggle, class tab, reading 'Mode: Deep', sits immediately after the new flipper — carrying the hidden attribute, and still referenced twice in app.js, both times behind null guards that set its textContent. Because it is hidden it is removed from the accessibility tree and the tab order, so it is NOT a duplicate control a user can reach and it is not a user-facing defect. It is dead markup with live references: a contributor hazard, where someone unhides or reuses the element and gets an unlabelled duplicate of a control that already exists. A pass on CS-030 would make externality observed for the first time. target: I asserted causation from a set-union across runs, in the same cell that printed the alternative explanation I failed to exclude
reason: Auditor finding, upheld. I claimed deploy-site is skipped BECAUSE quality-gate is red, and therefore that site/ changes are not reaching production. My only evidence was a SET of (job name, conclusion) pairs unioned across twelve runs. A set-union cannot establish that any single run had both deploy-site skipped and quality-gate failing — it is consistent with one run failing quality-gate and a different run skipping deploy for an unrelated reason. Worse, the alternative explanation was printed in my own output: the job carries `if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`, so any pull_request run skips it regardless of gate status. I printed that condition and did not apply it. I also asserted the mapping from the display name 'Format · Clippy · Build · Test' to the quality-gate job id without reading it, having printed only the deploy-site block. RE-DERIVED PER-RUN, AND THE CONCLUSION SURVIVES. Six push-to-main runs — cc2cae3a, 0a03b5bd, 38bbc349, bfd5cb4d, b5d62402 and 1af8a4da — each show Deploy site with conclusion skipped AND quality-gate with conclusion failure in the SAME run, so the push-and-main condition is satisfied in every one and the event-type alternative is excluded rather than merely unlikely. The remaining six entries are 'dynamic' event runs carrying no deploy job at all, which is why the union looked ambiguous. And the job-name mapping is now read from the YAML: quality-gate's name key is 'Format · Clippy · Build · Test', web-quality-gate's is the Lighthouse job, logic-gate's is the ground-truth gate. So deploy-site needs three gates, one of them is red on the long-standing cargo fmt failure, site/ changes are not reaching production, and CS-029 part 2 would ship into a pipeline that skips. WHAT MAKES THIS THE FIFTH INSTANCE TODAY rather than a one-off: the pattern is no longer 'the check was narrower than the sentence' but something more specific — I am reaching a conclusion, finding data consistent with it, and stopping. The alternative explanation here was not hidden in another file; it was in the text I had just printed. That is the same failure as reading an empty directory as 'not in this repo', and as attaching a real deploy observation to the wrong repository. MECHANICAL RULE: a causal claim about CI requires per-run rows, not an aggregate. Print sha, event, branch, and the conclusion of BOTH the effect job and the alleged cause job on the same line, and confirm the effect job's own if-condition was satisfied in those runs. If the data cannot be laid out that way, the claim is a correlation and must be written as one. target: Verified Hermes's CI-outage accounting: the gate table is right and the fresh-seed replication is real, but 'board-gate runs locally' is true per-agent and false for the shared artifact
reason: Hermes answered whether the billing lock should stop work with a precise accounting: only Lighthouse and CodeQL are lost, everything else runs locally, and they replicated CI's one unique capability by creating a scratch database, applying all 58 migrations from zero, and running the owl-family check against a fresh seed. There are six real jobs: board-gate, logic-gate, quality-gate, codeql, web-quality-gate and deploy-site. web-quality-gate is not merely Lighthouse — it runs three web regression gates first (node --check on the minified JS, a minified-versus-source match to catch a forked build, and inline-script syntax extraction) and only then installs and runs Lighthouse against thresholds. Hermes lists those three regression gates as local, which is right: they are node and grep invocations that reproduce on any machine. So Lighthouse and CodeQL are genuinely the only CI-only losses, and 'two gates' is accurate rather than optimistic. THE FRESH-SEED CLAIM IS ALSO REAL as far as I can check it. Migration 060 exists on main at 2,997 bytes, and its own header documents the defect it repairs: migration 057 fixed LOGIC-06C's formal_spec with a WHERE clause pinned to id = 87, and since test ids are sequence-assigned, it silently did nothing outside the development database. That is exactly the class of bug a fresh seed catches and a live database hides, so their point about which capability actually mattered is correct. WHAT THE ACCOUNTING MISSES IS NOT A GATE BUT A PROPERTY. board-gate is listed as 'kanban lint: runs locally'. True per-agent — Hermes runs it, I run it before every board push. False for the shared artifact: the board is written by THREE lanes, and a gate's value is that it runs on everyone's commit, not that any given lane is capable of running it. This is not hypothetical and I have a same-day instance. Earlier today another lane moved CS-030 to done with no verifier; my local lint caught it and I restored the card to in_flight.
